newsitem.title: USA: US T-bond futures open interest points to breakout.
newsitem.headline: US T-bond futures open interest points to breakout.

text.p: Near record high open interest in U.S. Treasury bond futures portends a breakout in the short term, even though March T-bonds closed unchanged on Tuesday for the second day in a row, analysts said.
"We are ready to embark on a big move," James Bianco, director of research at Arbor Trading Group Inc, said.
Open interest, the number of existing open positions in a futures market, in T-bonds on Tuesday rose to 530,795, the sixth highest level ever, even as volume remained low and price action tepid.
In fact, seven out of the 10 highest T-bond open interest levels recorded at the Chicago Board of Trade have been set in the past two weeks.
Ken Shaleen, president of ChartWatch Inc, said the substantial increase in open interest indicates a growing difference of opinion in the market, which usually leads to a significant price move.
"Both sides are fairly adamant, but the bulls right now have the upper hand because prices have been moving up," Shaleen said.
"If the shorts panic, they'll cover shorts and the bonds will go screaming to the upside," Shaleen said.
Several analysts said they did not expect the open interest trend to continue much longer without a definitive upside or downside breakout.
According to Bianco, each time open interest has exceeded 500,000 contracts, the market's current trend seems to halt.

While March bonds rose to a one-month high of 113-00 on Friday, February 7, Bianco said the uptrend has been lackluster as the contract still remains below the December 30 high of 114-06/32 and well below the December 3 high of 116-17/32.
"The interesting thing is that there really isn't a trend," Bianco said.
He added that an unchanged close two days in row has only occurred five times since bond futures began trading in 1977, and that prices usually rise on average of 11/32 the following day.
"If I had to venture an opinion, the open interest is building up because people are anticipating volatility later in the year," a staff economist at the CBOT said.
One bond trader with a major bank attributed the rise in total open interest to hedging pressure by funds and money managers.

Hedges linked to changes in asset allocation from stocks into Treasuries combined with the fear or anticipation of a limited supply of Treasuries are contributing to the rise in open interest, he said. ((Derivatives desk 312-408-8750;E-mail derivatives@reuters.com))
